title: Vayishlach: too small (Genesis 32:11)
hook: Jacob prays "I am not worthy of all the mercies"
carry: too small for all this kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahanaim, two camps. Your line was angels at every border. This week: Esau's tears, a town dimmer when Jacob left, a ladder in a plain place, a tenth, a stone moved by love, and angels at the edges. Today, a new portion. Day one hundred ninety-six.

You're about to see someone you wronged a long time ago. A sibling, an ex, an old friend. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times. And then you hear they're coming, and they're bringing a crowd. This week's portion is called Vayishlach, and he sent. Jacob sends messengers ahead to his brother Esau, twenty years after he took his blessing. The messengers come back with news: Esau is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him. Today: too small.
screen: `THE PERSON YOU WRONGED.` → `VAYISHLACH: AND HE SENT.` → `FOUR HUNDRED MEN.`

segments.voice: The Torah says Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. Two words, and Rashi says they mean two different fears: afraid he'd be killed, and distressed that he might have to kill. He splits his people into two camps, so that if one is attacked, the other can escape. And then he prays. It's one of the first long prayers anyone says in the Torah, and it's worth hearing how it goes. He begins with God's names: God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac. He reminds God of the promise: you told me, go home, and I'll do you good. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, this: "I am not worthy of all the mercies" and all the faithfulness you've shown your servant. In Hebrew it's one word: katonti. I am small. I've become too small for all of this. With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, he says, and now I've become two camps. Think about who's saying this. Jacob, rich now, a big family, a man who's wrestled his way through twenty years. And his first move in danger isn't to list what he deserves. It's to say: I'm small, and I've been given so much. Only after that does he ask. Save me, please, from my brother's hand, because I'm afraid of him. Plain fear, said out loud. Jewish tradition has often held up this prayer as a model. Gratitude first, honesty about being small, and then a direct request. Being small, here, isn't shame. It's what makes the kindness visible.
screen: `AFRAID AND DISTRESSED.` · `GOD OF MY FATHERS, YOU PROMISED.` · `KATONTI: I AM SMALL.` · `SAVE ME: I AM AFRAID.` · then, large: `I AM NOT WORTHY OF ALL THE MERCIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for help, and admit your smallness. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you have that you once didn't: people, a roof, a skill, another morning. Let yourself feel small next to it, the good kind of small. Then name the thing you're afraid of right now, plainly. If you pray, you can use Jacob's words, I am not worthy of all the mercies, and then ask for help. If you don't, just hold both: the gifts and the fear. The bell holds the time.
Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion where Jacob, afraid of meeting his brother, prays that he's too small for all the kindness he's been shown.
Your line: too small for all this kindness. Today, before you ask for anything, from God or from anyone, first name one kindness you've already been given. Day one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: The shape of Jacob's prayer, praise and thanks first and then a request, echoes the structure of the Amidah, the central Jewish prayer, which opens by naming the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
